hero.headline: Watermarking 101
hero.sub: Claude now watermarks its text using Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text. There are no hidden characters to strip. The watermark is the word choice itself. Here's the mechanism, running live on whatever you type.

items.text: Watermarking is centuries old. Two kinds: visible (think logos across stock photos), and invisible (only special tools can see it).
Anthropic rolled out the invisible kind for text in August 2026, using SynthID-Text.
It works on word choice, not hidden characters. Copy-pasting it anywhere changes nothing.
Detection isn't public. Anthropic only grants it to organizations eligible under EU law: regulators, law enforcement, media, fact-checkers, independent researchers, and similar groups.

explainer.heading: Two kinds of words, one sentence
explainer.intro: Every word Claude generates is one of two things: a fixed word, or a tournament word. Watch this watermarked sentence generate, one word at a time, and see which is which.
explainer.sentence: Smart teams test ideas fast, then ship what works.
explainer.payoff: Multiply this across a full paragraph and that pattern of choices becomes detectable. That pattern is the watermark. Try it on your own text below.

simulator.heading: The tournament sampling simulator
simulator.intro: Type or paste anything below. Every word with a plausible alternative competes in a small tournament, seeded by your key and the words right before it. Change the key and watch every outcome change.
simulator.textareaHint: Pretend this is text an AI just wrote, since that's what actually gets watermarked. Not a prompt you'd type to an AI, the output it would hand back.
simulator.disclaimer: Simulation. This runs the same mechanism on a demo key, not Anthropic's key. It cannot detect real Claude text.
simulator.mechanismNote: The real SynthID-Text samples candidates from the model's full probability distribution over its vocabulary and runs a multi-layer knockout tournament. This demo swaps in a small, fixed dictionary of 2 to 5 alternatives per word, so you can see the mechanism run in a browser.

meaning.heading: What this means for your team

items.text: Factual writing carries less watermark because there are fewer possible word choices.

A reliable general AI detector fails to exist. This isn't the same thing as a third-party "AI detector." Those tools guess statistically and get it wrong often: one Stanford study found they falsely flagged more than 60% of essays by non-native English speakers as AI-written.

Nobody outside Anthropic knows yet what a real watermark result will actually look like: a percentage, a plain yes or no, who gets to run the check, or whose hands the answer ends up in. The watermark itself carries no other metadata either, no account, no model version, nothing beyond the signal.
This exists partly because regulators required it. Article 50 of the EU AI Act mandates machine-readable marking of AI-generated content, and providers who skip it face real penalties.

items.heading: Why now
items.body: Article 50 of the EU AI Act requires providers to mark AI-generated content in a machine-readable format. Its Code of Practice already has roughly 190 signatories, so most model providers are building their own version of this.

items.heading: Images and files work differently
items.body: Pictures and documents get C2PA content credentials in their metadata instead of a text watermark. That's a weaker guarantee, since metadata is easy to strip.

items.heading: "The quality cost," worth a caveat
items.body: Google measured a 0.01% difference in thumbs-up across roughly 20 million Gemini responses, a gap small enough to be statistically insignificant. Worth noting: thumbs-up is a crude, self-selected signal. Most responses never get rated at all, and it's not built to catch subtle shifts or comparison in word choice.

goDeeper.heading: Go deeper
goDeeper.note: A production implementation ships in Hugging Face Transformers v4.46.0 and later.

funFact.heading: Watermarks are hiding everywhere
funFact.body: Since the mid-1980s, most color laser printers and copiers have quietly added their own watermark: a grid of near-invisible yellow dots on every page, encoding the printer's serial number and the date and time it printed. Xerox and Canon built it so counterfeiters could be traced back to a specific machine, and nobody outside the printer industry knew the dots existed until 2004.

items.q: Can you remove a Claude watermark by copy-pasting the text?
items.a: No. There are no hidden characters, invisible Unicode, or metadata involved. The watermark is the specific words the model chose, and copying or pasting text doesn't change a single word, so it doesn't touch the signal at all.

items.q: How long does the text need to be for detection to work?
items.a: Neither Anthropic nor Google publishes a minimum word count, but the pattern is consistent: longer passages give the detector more watermarked words to average over, which raises confidence. Very short snippets, like a one-line caption, generally won't carry enough signal to register.

Barely, and that's expected. Code has exact syntax with very few interchangeable word choices, so there's little room to apply a word-choice watermark. However, inline comments within code (and likely pull requests) will carry a full watermark since they involve normal language choices, the same as translations of text.

items.q: Can it tell who wrote something, or which specific person or chat it came from?
items.a: No. The watermark carries no identifying information. It cannot be traced to a user, an organization, or a specific conversation, and it can't confirm human authorship or identify other AI systems either.

items.q: Does watermarking hurt Claude's output quality?
items.a: Google's own measurement, across roughly 20 million Gemini responses using the same SynthID-Text approach, found a 0.01% difference in thumbs-up, small enough to be statistically insignificant. Take that with a grain of salt though: thumbs-up is a crude, self-selected metric, not built to catch subtle shifts or comparison in word choice, and it's not a great measurement of quality to begin with. There's no added cost, no added tokens, and no meaningful speed impact.

items.q: If Claude only edits my draft instead of writing it, does the watermark still apply?
items.a: Only to the words Claude actually changed. If Claude lightly edits a paragraph you wrote, the watermark lives in those specific edits, which may be too few words to register with any confidence.
